entries.topicDescription: Working effectively with Kotlin's type system, nullability, and smart casts.

tips.title: The safe call operator ?. short-circuits instead of throwing
tips.content:
Calling a method or property on a null reference in most languages throws
an exception immediately. Kotlin's ?. operator checks for null first —
if the receiver is null, the whole expression evaluates to null instead of
crashing, and the call is simply skipped.

Safe calls chain naturally: `user?.address?.city` returns null at the
first null link in the chain, without needing a nested if-null check at
every step.
tips.codeSnippet:
val name: String? = user?.profile?.displayName
// if user or profile is null, name is null — no crash, no nested if-checks

tips.title: isNullOrEmpty and isNullOrBlank combine a null check with a content check
tips.content:
Checking `if (str != null && str.isEmpty())` for a nullable string is
verbose, and it's easy to forget one half of the check.

isNullOrEmpty() (empty string or null) and isNullOrBlank() (also treats
whitespace-only strings as empty) combine both checks into a single call —
and because they're written with a contract, the compiler still smart-casts
the string to non-null afterward when used in a negated check.

tips.title: Nullability is part of the type itself: String vs String?
tips.content:
In many languages, whether a value can be null is a runtime concern you
discover through documentation or a crash. In Kotlin, String and String?
are genuinely different types — the compiler refuses to compile code that
treats a String? as if it were guaranteed non-null without a check.

This pushes null-handling decisions to compile time: a function signature
like `fun greet(name: String)` documents, and enforces, that null is never
a valid argument — callers get a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
tips.codeSnippet:
fun greet(name: String) = println("Hello, $name") // name can never be null here

fun greetOptional(name: String?) = println("Hello, ${name ?: "stranger"}") // must handle null explicitly

tips.title: Smart casts don't work on mutable properties from another class
tips.content:
The compiler can only guarantee a null-checked var stays non-null if it
can prove nothing else could reassign it between the check and the use —
that guarantee breaks for a mutable property accessed through another
object, since another thread or a getter with custom logic could change it.

Copy the property to a local val first — the local val is guaranteed
unchanged, so the smart cast works normally on it.

tips.title: Elvis operator with return/throw for early-exit null handling
tips.content:
Chaining multiple ?.let blocks to handle a nullable value gets hard to read
fast, especially when you need to bail out of the function on null.

Combine ?: with return or throw directly at the point of null-checking —
this reads top-to-bottom like a guard clause and keeps the rest of the
function body working with a guaranteed non-null value.

tips.title: The platform type gap when calling Java from Kotlin
tips.content:
Java has no concept of nullability annotations Kotlin can always trust, so
values returned from Java code show up as platform types (String! rather
than String or String?) — Kotlin lets you treat them as either, which
defeats the compiler's null-safety guarantees at that boundary.

Wrap Java API calls in an explicit null check or a Kotlin-native adapter
layer as soon as they cross into your Kotlin code, so a NullPointerException
from unannotated Java code doesn't surface deep inside otherwise-safe
Kotlin logic.

tips.title: !! is a debugging tool, not a production null-handling strategy
tips.content:
The not-null assertion operator converts a null into an immediate
NullPointerException with a generic message and no context about which
value was null or why.

Every !! in code that ships is a place where a null will crash the app
with no recovery path and a poor stack trace. Prefer requireNotNull(x) {
"message" } for preconditions (clearer failure message) or checkNotNull for
invariants, and reserve !! for cases you've proven structurally impossible.

tips.title: Contracts let custom null-check functions enable smart casts
tips.content:
By default, only the compiler's built-in null checks (if (x != null)) and
a handful of stdlib functions trigger smart casts — a custom function like
fun isValid(x: String?): Boolean won't let the compiler smart-cast after
calling it, even if the logic is equivalent.

The contract {} DSL lets you declare that a function implies a certain
nullability outcome, teaching the compiler to smart-cast after calling your
own validation functions, not just built-in ones.

tips.title: Nothing type marks functions that never return normally
tips.content:
A function that always throws or always loops forever has return type
Nothing, which the compiler treats as a subtype of every other type — this
lets it slot into any expression position without breaking type inference.

Declaring TODO() or a custom fatalError() as returning Nothing lets you
write `val x = condition ?: fatalError("...")` and have x inferred as
non-nullable, because the compiler knows the Nothing branch can never
actually produce a value.

tips.title: Safe call operator (?.)
tips.content:
The safe call operator ?. lets you access properties or call methods 
on a nullable reference. If the object is null, the entire expression 
returns null instead of throwing a NullPointerException.

You can chain multiple safe calls together. 
If any part in the chain is null, the whole chain short-circuits to null.

This replaces verbose if-null checks from Java.

tips.title: Elvis operator (?:)
tips.content:
The Elvis operator ?: provides a default value when an expression is null.
The name comes from the emoticon — tilt your head left and ?: looks like Elvis' hair.

It's perfect for fallback values and early returns.
You can even use 'return' or 'throw' on the right side 
to exit a function when something is null.

tips.title: Smart casts after null checks
tips.content:
Kotlin's compiler tracks null checks and automatically casts 
the variable to its non-null type within the checked scope. 
This is called "smart casting".

After an if-check, return, or throw, the compiler knows the variable 
can't be null and lets you use it without ?. operators.

Smart casts only work on val (immutable) variables — 
a var could be changed by another thread between the check and usage.

tips.title: Definitely non-nullable types (T & Any) tighten generic Java interop
tips.content:
A generic type parameter with no explicit bound is treated as nullable
(T?) by default in certain override scenarios involving platform types
from Java generics, which can force a nullable parameter type even when
your Kotlin code logically never passes null.

`T & Any` (definitely non-nullable) explicitly intersects a type
parameter with Any, guaranteeing non-nullability regardless of how T is
instantiated — mainly useful when overriding a generic Java method whose
nullability annotations are ambiguous or absent.
tips.codeSnippet:
fun <T> elvisNonNull(value: T, fallback: T & Any): T & Any =
    value ?: fallback // return type is guaranteed non-null regardless of T's nullability

tips.title: Combine as? with the Elvis operator for a safe-cast-with-default idiom
tips.content:
Using `as` for an unchecked cast throws a ClassCastException immediately
if the value isn't actually the target type — risky when a value's exact
type isn't guaranteed, such as after JSON deserialization into a
heterogeneous structure.

`as?` returns null instead of throwing on a failed cast, and chaining it
with `?:` gives you a one-line safe-cast-with-fallback idiom, avoiding a
separate `is` check followed by a smart cast.
tips.codeSnippet:
val config: Map<String, Any> = loadConfig()
val timeout = (config["timeout"] as? Int) ?: 30_000 // safe cast, default on mismatch or absence

tips.title: ::isInitialized checks a lateinit property without triggering the exception
tips.content:
Accessing an uninitialized lateinit property throws
UninitializedPropertyAccessException — but sometimes you genuinely need
to check whether it's been set yet without risking that exception, such
as in a cleanup path that may run before setup completes.

The reflective `this::property.isInitialized` check (available since
Kotlin 1.2 for properties in the same scope) returns a Boolean safely,
letting you branch on initialization state without a try/catch.

tips.title: Extension functions can be defined on nullable receivers
tips.content:
A regular extension function like `fun String.isValid()` can only be
called on a non-null String — calling it on a String? forces a safe call
or a null check first, spreading null-handling logic across every call
site.

Defining the extension on the nullable type directly (`fun String?.isValid()
`) lets the function itself decide how to handle a null receiver
internally, centralizing that null-handling logic in one place instead of
repeating it at every call site.

tips.title: Unsafe as throws ClassCastException; as? swallows the failure into null
tips.content:
It's tempting to treat `as` and `as?` as interchangeable style choices,
but they have fundamentally different failure modes: `as` fails loudly
(an immediate exception with a stack trace pointing at the exact line),
while `as?` fails silently into null, which can propagate a missing value
far from where the actual type mismatch occurred.

Use `as` when a type mismatch represents a genuine programming bug you
want to surface immediately; use `as?` only when an unexpected type is a
normal, expected possibility your code already handles gracefully
downstream.
tips.codeSnippet:
val value: Any = fetchDynamicValue()

val strict = value as String // crashes loudly if wrong — bug should be visible
val lenient = value as? String ?: "default" // wrong type treated as a normal case

tips.title: requireNotNull documents a precondition; checkNotNull documents an invariant
tips.content:
Both functions throw if given null and otherwise return the non-null
value, so they're functionally similar — but they throw different
exception types and communicate different intent to a reader.

requireNotNull throws IllegalArgumentException and is meant for validating
inputs the caller provided (a precondition on arguments); checkNotNull
throws IllegalStateException and is meant for asserting your own code's
internal state is as expected (an invariant) — picking the right one
communicates whose bug it would be if the check fails.

tips.title: @Nullable/@NonNull Java annotations determine platform type strictness
tips.content:
When Kotlin calls Java code without JSR-305 or JetBrains nullability
annotations, every return type is an unchecked platform type — but if the
Java code IS annotated (@Nullable, @NonNull, or JSR-305 equivalents),
Kotlin respects those annotations and treats the type as genuinely
nullable or non-nullable at compile time, not as an ambiguous platform
type.

When writing Java code that Kotlin consumers will call — including
annotation-processor-generated Java, which is common in Android — adding
nullability annotations meaningfully improves the calling Kotlin code's
type safety instead of forcing every caller into platform-type ambiguity.

tips.title: A smart cast can be invalidated across a suspension point
tips.content:
A local val smart-cast to non-null normally stays valid for the rest of
its scope — but if that val is actually a property backed by a mutable
field accessed through a class captured in a suspend lambda, a
suspension point in between can theoretically allow another coroutine to
mutate the underlying value, so the compiler is conservative about
smart-casting across suspend calls in shared mutable state scenarios.

Copying a nullable property into an immutable local val before any
suspend call, and using only that local val afterward, avoids this class
of invalidation entirely, since a true local val can't be reassigned by
another coroutine.

tips.title: Nullable function types need extra parentheses to express correctly
tips.content:
`(() -> Unit)?` and `() -> Unit?` look similar but mean different things:
the first is a nullable reference to a function that returns Unit; the
second is a non-nullable function that itself returns a nullable Unit
value (which is a nonsensical but legal type).

Getting the parentheses placement wrong is a common source of confusing
compiler errors when defining callback parameters that are genuinely
optional (may not be provided at all, as opposed to always being called
but sometimes returning null).
tips.codeSnippet:
var onComplete: (() -> Unit)? = null // the callback itself may be absent
onComplete?.invoke() // safe call needed since the reference itself might be null

fun risky(): () -> Unit? = { null } // rarely what you actually want

tips.title: Exhaustive when on a nullable sealed type must handle the null branch separately
tips.content:
A `when` expression over a sealed type's non-null variant is exhaustive
once every subtype is covered — but if the variable's type is the
nullable version of that sealed type (MySealedType?), the compiler also
requires an explicit `null ->` branch, since null isn't one of the sealed
subtypes and wouldn't otherwise be covered.

This is a common source of a 'when expression must be exhaustive' compile
error when a previously non-nullable sealed-typed property becomes
nullable during a refactor — the fix is adding the null branch, not
changing the sealed hierarchy.
